L976@P31: 4.3.5. Data Protection Level
L977@P31: Varying data protection policies may be established within an organization. For example, an
L978@P31: organization can have an engineering department and a sales department, where the sales
L979@P31: personnel do not need to access detailed proprietary technical data (e.g., source code,
L980@P31: schematics), and the engineers do not need to access the PII of the organization’s customers.
L981@P31: Both might be within the same confidentiality categorization but are contextually different and
L982@P31: have different internal and external rules regarding necessary controls. As such, the data
L983@P31: protection level is a complementary consideration to organizational control. When identifying
L984@P31: whether sanitization is necessary, both organizational control and the data protection level
L985@P31: should be considered.
L986@P31: 4.3.6. Sanitization and Disposal Decision
L987@P31: Once an organization completes an assessment of its system confidentiality, determines the
L988@P31: need for information sanitization, determines appropriate time frames for sanitization, and
L989@P31: determines the types of media used and the media disposition, then an effective, risk-based
L990@P31: decision can be made on the appropriate and needed level of sanitization (see IEEE 2883.1 [22]
L991@P31: for additional guidance). Again, certain factors and media types might cause the sanitization
L992@P31: method to change.
L993@P31: Once a sanitization decision has been made, the organization should record the decision and
L994@P31: ensure that a process and proper resources are in place to support that decision. The process
L995@P31: includes the act of sanitization as well as verification, including decisions, actions, resources,
L996@P31: and critical interfaces with key officials.
L997@P31: 4.4. Performing Sanitization
L998@P31: After the requirement to sanitize media has been established, the sanitization should be
L999@P31: performed based on the selected sanitization method (i.e., clear, purge, or destroy) and in a
L1000@P31: manner that complies with IEEE 2883 [13].
L1001@P31: 15
L1002@P31: 15 The IEEE 2883 series provides additional information about selecting appropriate sanitization methods for use, as well as technology-specific
L1003@P31: sanitization techniques.
L1004@P31: or a standard that is identified as acceptable by
L1005@P31: organizational policy (e.g., NSA/CSS Policy 6-22 [17], NSA/CSS Policy Manual 9-12 [16]).
L1006@P31: Depending on the media type (i.e., hard copy or ISM) and selected sanitization method, there
L1007@P31: can be multiple sanitization technique options. The option that provides the most
L1008@P31: confidentiality protection should be used. When the purge sanitization technique of CE is used
L1009@P31: for an ISM, Sec. 3.2 should be consulted for additional considerations or requirements.
L1010@P31: As part of performing the sanitization, certain details will need to be captured, including the
L1011@P31: results/outcomes of the sanitization (see Sec. 4.5), the information necessary to document the
L1012@P31: sanitization (see Sec. 4.6), and other relevant information.
L1013@P31: The proper initial configuration of each ISM helps ensure that the sanitization operation is as
L1014@P31: effective as possible. The individuals performing the sanitization are encouraged to check
L1015@P31-32: manufacturer recommendations and guides, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency NIST SP 800-88r2 Guidelines for Media Sanitization
L1016@P32: September 2025
L1017@P32: 24
L1018@P32: Security (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIGs) [21], for additional
L1019@P32: information about recommended settings. Sanitization techniques typically play no role in
L1020@P32: configuring ISM. A frequent misconception is that a sanitized ISM will resemble a factory-fresh
L1021@P32: drive (i.e., in a factory default state), but this is often not the case. Additional configuration
L1022@P32: changes may be necessary before the ISM can be readily reused.
L1023@P32: 4.5. Sanitization Assurance
L1024@P32: Per ISO/IEC 27040 [15], verifying the adequacy or effectiveness of sanitization outcomes is an
L1025@P32: important aspect of a media sanitization program. The results of attempted sanitization
L1026@P32: techniques are inspected (see Sec. 4.5.1), and a decision on the adequacy of the results is made
L1027@P32: (see Sec. 4.5.2). These activities are shown as the “Validate” decision point in Fig. 1. If the
L1028@P32: outcomes are expected and appropriate, the sanitization is accepted. If outcomes are not
L1029@P32: acceptable, then sanitization is repeated. Repeated sanitization should recheck the reusability
L1030@P32: of media because a previous sanitization technique may have rendered the media unusable or
L1031@P32: inoperable.
L1032@P32: 4.5.1. Sanitization Verification
L1033@P32: The goal of sanitization verification is to determine the outcome of the sanitization technique
L1034@P32: used during the sanitization operation. The sanitization results should be inspected to verify
L1035@P32: that the sanitization technique was completed successfully.
L1036@P32: For destructive sanitization methods applied to either hard copy or ISM, this verification
L1037@P32: involves inspecting the remnants of a destruction technique and identifying the equipment
L1038@P32: used with it.
L1039@P32: For non-destructive sanitization methods for ISM, verification can be more complex and
L1040@P32: typically depends on the type of ISM. Clear and logical purge sanitization techniques that
L1041@P32: involve tools and systems can be verified by checking the completion status of the tools and
L1042@P32: identifying errors, anomalies, and the health of the ISM. For physical purge sanitization
L1043@P32: techniques, the equipment performing the sanitization should be checked to confirm that it
L1044@P32: completed its operation successfully. The ISM may not be in a usable state until certain device
L1045@P32: software and configurations are reestablished, so there can be limitations on further
L1046@P32: inspections of the ISM.
L1047@P32: Unless explicitly required by organizational policy, elaborate sampling of an ISM’s contents
L1048@P32: (e.g., full or representative) after clear or purge sanitization techniques is not necessary.
L1049@P32: 4.5.2. Sanitization Validation
L1050@P32: The goal of sanitization validation is to ensure that the target data was effectively sanitized.
L1051@P32: Sanitization validation results in a decision to either approve the sanitization as being effective
L1052@P32: or reject it, which would require repeating the sanitization method using a different sanitization
L1053@P32-33: technique or escalating to a more secure sanitization method. NIST SP 800-88r2 Guidelines for Media Sanitization
L1054@P33: September 2025
L1055@P33: 25
L1056@P33: The results of the sanitization verification are considered (see Sec. 4.5.1). Any identified errors,
L1057@P33: anomalies, or other issues should be analyzed, and risks to data confidentiality should be
L1058@P33: assessed. Unacceptable data confidentiality risks associated with the sanitization operation
L1059@P33: should result in the sanitization not being accepted (i.e., rejected) as sufficient to ensure the
L1060@P33: confidentiality of sensitive data (i.e., an additional sanitization method is needed).
L1061@P33: The effectiveness of the sanitization may be called into question by several other
L1062@P33: considerations, including:
L1063@P33: • The ISM may appear fully functional, but some portion of the ISM may no longer be
L1064@P33: accessible through the ISM’s interface due to errors or performance conditions.
L1065@P33: • The selected sanitization method and/or technique is not appropriate for the media or
L1066@P33: the security category of the information. For example, a sanitization operation that
L1067@P33: degausses an SSD can complete successfully, but no sensitive data is sanitized.
L1068@P33: • The sanitization may have been performed by unqualified personnel, or the tools and/or
L1069@P33: equipment used were not approved and/or were improperly calibrated.
L1070@P33: • The outcome does not meet minimum requirements. For example, a shredder is used
L1071@P33: on an optical disc and results in pieces that are 50 % larger than what is acceptable to
L1072@P33: the organization. The sanitization technique completed successfully but is not
L1073@P33: considered effective.
L1074@P33: • The scope of the sanitization (i.e., target data) was too narrowly focused. For example,
L1075@P33: an ISM that employs overprovisioning is sanitized using clear sanitization technique
L1076@P33: based on simple writes to overwrite existing contents and potentially leaves a
L1077@P33: substantial amount of user data unchanged.
L1078@P33: The validation process considers the sanitization outcomes and the sensitivity of the target data
L1079@P33: and decides (shown as “Validate” in Fig. 1) whether the target data has been sanitized to an
L1080@P33: acceptable level (i.e., the organization accepts any residual risks). In other words, the level of
L1081@P33: effort that is necessary to potentially gain access to the data after the sanitization operation is
L1082@P33: deemed sufficient to ensure the confidentiality of the data.
L1083@P33: 4.6. Documentation
L1084@P33: Following sanitization, a certificate of sanitization (see Appendix C) should be completed for
L1085@P33: each ISM that has been sanitized, per the organization’s policies. A certification of sanitization
L1086@P33: may be a physical (e.g., piece of paper) or electronic record of the action taken. For example,
L1087@P33: some ISM include bar codes on the label for the model and serial numbers, so the person
L1088@P33: performing the sanitization might simply enter the details into a tracking application and scan
L1089@P33: each bar code as the ISM is sanitized. Automatic documentation can be important as some
L1090@P33: systems make physical access to the ISM very difficult.
L1091@P33: When fully completed, the certificate should record at least the following details:
L1092@P33-34: • ManufacturerNIST SP 800-88r2 Guidelines for Media Sanitization

L1095@P34: • Model
L1096@P34: • Serial number
L1097@P34: • Organizationally assigned media or property number (if applicable)
L1098@P34: • Media type (i.e., hard copy or ISM)
L1099@P34: • Media source (e.g., user, computer)
L1100@P34: • Pre-sanitization confidentiality categorization (optional)
L1101@P34: • Sanitization method (i.e., clear, purge, destroy)
L1102@P34: • Sanitization technique (e.g., degauss, overwrite, block erase, CE)
L1103@P34: • Tool used, including version
L1104@P34: • Verification method
L1105@P34: • Information of individuals performing verification and validation:
L1106@P34: o Name of person

L1108@P34: o Date
L1109@P34: o Location
L1110@P34: o Contact information (e.g., phone number)
L1111@P34: o Signature
L1112@P34: If the ISM has been successfully validated (see Sec. 4.5) and the sanitization results in a lower
L1113@P34: confidentiality level for the ISM, all markings on the ISM that indicate the previous
L1114@P34: confidentiality level should be removed.
L1115@P34: The value of a certification of media disposition depends on the organization’s handling of ISM
L1116@P34: over the ISM’s life cycle. The organization can most effectively identify how well ISM
L1117@P34: sanitization is being applied across the enterprise if records are maintained when the ISM is
L1118@P34: introduced to the environment, when it leaves the place where it was last used, and when it
L1119@P34: reaches the post-sanitization destination. If there is a breakdown in tracking at locations other
L1120@P34: than the post-sanitization destination, sanitization records will only show that specific ISM were
L1121@P34: sanitized and not whether the organization is effectively sanitizing all ISM that have been
L1122@P34: introduced into the operating environment.
L1123@P34: 4.7. Roles and Responsibilities
L1124@P34: A successful media sanitization program depends on the sustained efforts and oversight of
L1125@P34: many individuals, and this section describes example roles and responsibilities. These roles
L1126@P34: focus on assuring programmatic success as opposed to operational responsibilities, which are
L1127@P34-35: not addressed.NIST SP 800-88r2 Guidelines for Media Sanitization

L1130@P35: 4.7.1. Program Managers/Agency Heads
L1131@P35: Program managers are responsible for establishing an effective information security
L1132@P35: governance structure, including the organization’s computer security program and its overall
L1133@P35: goals, objectives, and priorities. Agency heads are responsible for providing adequate resources
L1134@P35: to the program to ensure its success. Allocated resources should correctly identify the types
L1135@P35: and locations of information.
